normalization.overview: A developer reports running a 284-billion-parameter model on a CPU-only laptop. The engineering is interesting. The unanswered question is what survives the compression.
normalization.whyItMatters: Extreme quantization and sparse model activation may shift local compute feasibility, but tokens per second do not measure retained intelligence.
normalization.ghostMeshTakeaway: Reproduce the exact CPU-only workload and compare quality to matched higher-precision and smaller-model baselines before treating model size as an operational advantage.
normalization.falsification: Reproduce the hardware/software configuration and compare task-specific accuracy, reliability, latency, context prefill, memory headroom and cost against higher-precision and smaller models.
normalization.freshness: November 9 video cutoff; newer project repository quality and platform claims are distinct and not independently verified here.

claims.proposition: A developer reported a CPU-only 284B model at approximately 9–10 tokens per second.
claims.assessment: Video introduces and qualifies the reported result.

claims.proposition: The MoE model has roughly 284B total / 13B active parameters and a reported 1.71-bit compressed representation.
claims.assessment: Video describes sparse activation, memory fit and custom code.
claims.limits: Compressed fidelity relative to higher precision not established.

claims.proposition: Developer reports distinct prefill, decode and speculative-decoding rates.
claims.assessment: Video distinguishes approximately 43–44 prefill, 9–10 decode and higher speculative peaks.

claims.proposition: Low-bit compression does not by itself prove retained original model capability.
claims.assessment: Video questions quality retention at extreme compression.
claims.limits: No matched higher-precision full-weight capability evaluation.

claims.proposition: AVX-512, memory headroom, patched software and missing independent replication limit broad usability.
claims.assessment: Video describes hardware and software caveats.
claims.limits: As-of video cutoff; newer repo claims must be assessed separately.

claims.proposition: Memory capacity and memory bandwidth constrain practical CPU inference differently.
claims.assessment: Video examines hardware prerequisites and bandwidth.
claims.limits: Specific systems and workloads will differ.

claims.proposition: A developer experiment is not yet a broadly qualified local inference tool.
claims.assessment: Video distinguishes demo from operational utility and smaller high-precision alternatives.
claims.limits: Product judgment and recommended independent tests are GhostMesh synthesis.

relationships.reason: An attractive demonstration cannot stand in for qualified model capability; this experiment tests that distinction at extreme quantization.
Inference economics must include actual workload, waiting time and operator constraints, not only model size or peak token rates.
Local execution gives control over placement but not automatic independence from specialized software, validation and source provenance.
